label: The problem
show: Five dots, one turns amber. A bar: 4 in 10 get treatment. Then a thin line that slips down over weeks and fades.
text: One in five American teenagers goes through depression in a year, and most get no treatment. It builds slowly: a little less sleep, fewer texts, dropped plans. So nobody sees it.

label: What we built
show: The Steady mark draws itself. Two phones slide in: Maya's and her mom's.
text: So we built Steady. It lives on a teenager's phone, linked to a parent's. Meet Maya.

label: It learns her normal
show: Maya's phone in the centre. The ring fills over four weeks. The four signals light up as they are named. Then she taps the two-dot check-in.
text: For four weeks, Steady learns what's normal for her: her sleep, how often she reaches out, how much she moves, and the tone of what she types. Once a week, she checks in with two taps.

label: It asks
show: Week four: the two questions come up and she answers low. Weeks five and six: the ring turns amber, her check-ins climb, the model's score crosses its line, and the questions come up again.
text: Every month, Steady asks two questions, the ones doctors use. Maya says she's mostly okay, and Steady takes her at her word. Then finals hit. Her check-ins get tense, and our model doesn't wait a month. It asks again.

label: The note
show: Week six she answers low again. Week eight her answers are high. Mom's phone slides in. An amber dot crosses from Maya's phone to hers and the note opens.
text: She still says she's fine. But at week eight, her answers come back high. Maya sees a nudge to see a doctor, and her mom gets a note: what changed, for how long, and how to start the conversation. Never her messages.

label: Her words stay on her phone
show: Maya types a message. It becomes a bubble, then a single dot. A counter holds at 0 bytes sent.
text: What Maya types never leaves her phone. A small model reads each message there, keeps one dot, and lets the words go.

label: Does it work: the tone model
show: Two bars grow: tone model 50%, keyword list 24%.
text: Does it work? On five thousand comments it had never seen, our tone model caught half of the low-mood ones. A keyword list caught a quarter.

label: Does it work: when to ask
show: 213 dots. 'Our first idea failed.' Then two bars: the ask model 44%, a fixed calendar 13%. Then: 113 teens, never seen, AUC 0.85.
text: Then we tested timing on phone data from two hundred thirteen students, and our first idea failed. Phone signals picked the week no better than chance. So we rebuilt Steady to ask first. Its model put forty-four percent of its asks on a hard week. A calendar: thirteen. And on a hundred thirteen teenagers it had never seen, it still held up.

label: What it can't do yet
show: Three short lines with icons: who, not yet which week; a crisis or a friend helping; a clinician.
text: It knows who to ask, not yet which week. Our self-harm model can't tell someone in crisis from a friend helping them. So on its own, it only asks, and it needs a clinician.

label: Close
show: The Steady mark, 'knowing when to ask', and 'Prototype. Not medical advice.'
text: Steady is a prototype, not medical advice. But asking at the right time could change who gets help.
